JAZZ ORAL HISTORY PROJECT
ORAL HISTORY - LEONARD PHILLIPS

Interviewer
Bryant Dupre
January 1983
Leonard Phillips (Interviewed by Bryant Dupre):

Here we are with Leonard "Phil" Phillips, and we're at Phil's apartment. It's right now January 26, 1983, Wednesday afternoon/early evening, up on 1400 Fairmont Street. We'd like to start at the beginning, Phil. Go back and talk about Arkansas. You wanted to start back then. Tell us about when you were born, your birthday and everything -- you know, family, early roots and all that.
Yeah. I was born in 1907, Warren, Arkansas.
And your birthday?

My birthday is the 4th of September. And, in 1921, it was a guy got a band together, a school band, and we started playing like that. His name was Professor Parson. He started us out. We got the band, he started us out in school playing. So I first started playing E-flat clarinet.
What school was that? Do you know the name of the school?
It was Myrtle Street School. He got a band together, we started rehearsing -- that was in 1921. Then in 1924, Lester Young's father came to my home town. He had a show there.
Willis Young.
Yeah, Willis Young. Billy Young.
They called him Billy?
Everybody called him Billy, yeah, in show
Phillips - 2

business. His show closed in my home, and he went up there, and he stayed there, in a big auditorium there, and he used to put on a show, say, twice the week -- maybe the first of the week and Friday he'd put on a show. And he used to... I got talkin' with him, and he told me to come up, he wanted to talk with me. He said, "I think you got some promise in making a musician." So I said, "Okay." That knocked me out, you know. I mean, I was lookin', because I wanted to advance myself.
So we... Pete Jones...
Pete Jones, a trombonist?
A trombonist. Pete Jones and my brother...
Your brother's first name is...?
Clarence. And several other guys around there. And we got the band... We got about ten pieces together. And he started rehearsing us.
Willis Young got all those people from Warren.
Yeah, everybody from Warren. Oh, no. Not him.
Oh, this was not Willis Young?
No, this... Yeah, I'm getting myself mixed up. Yeah, we would go up to his place, and he would talk to us, you know. He'd tell us all about music, what he did. He did...
Up at Willis Young's place.
In Warren.
Phillips - 3
In Warren.
In Warren, yeah.
Was Prez with him at that time?
Sure, everybody. Prez was only about 12 or 13 years old.
So he was just living up there?

He was living there for the winter. He stayed there for the winter. And while he was there, he was teaching us. We used to go up to his place. He used to teach me, he learned me how to play different tunes. Like "Wang, Wang Blues" -- that was a good tune in those days to play. "Wang, Wang Blues" and "You've Been A Good Old Wagon But You Done Broke Down." Show tunes, you know. Well, he taught us, and he was teaching the horn too. Teach the scales and everything.
So when he got ready to leave, he left and told my mother that he wanted me to go with him.
Prez was into scales, too?
No. Hell no. Prez played his ass off even then.
But was he doing scales?
Prez?
Yeah.
No!
He didn't work on scales.
Phillips - 4
No. Prez was that far ahead of us. He was already playing. See, he was playing. He was playing like he'd been playing for years.
But presumably, Willis Young would have gotten him into scales earlier on. Is that right?
No. Uh-unh. He didn't need to learn nothin' like that. He knew that.
There you go. That's what I was after.
Yeah!
So Prez... As far as you know, he wasn't into learning scales at any time.
No. He was way in advance of us. He could play anything he wanted to play. He had this on him, too -- a good ear. And he could play. Anything he'd hear, he could play it. You know what I mean?
So without going through all the practicing scales and...
He didn't have to practice. He was a guy that didn't practice much.
When you met him, that would have been 1924.
Yeah.
He was born in 1909. That would have made him... Let's see.
Maybe about 14 years old.
It would be 15 years old. [LESTER YOUNG WAS BORN AUGUST 27, 1909] So he was already good. And you never knew him to
Phillips - 5
practice. I mean, that's the first you knew him, and from that time on you never knew him to practice. Or did you? I'm just asking you.
Yeah. Well, when we got the band together, we practiced music. You know, to have some new music to go rehearse in the band.
I don't mean practicing music, but practicing the instrument.

Any time he'd practice his horn, he'd be playing some tune. He'd be playing some tune that he heard. You know what I mean? Tunes like in them days was out, was "Baby, Won't You Please Come Home?" and "Jada"(?), those tunes... But he was playin' them tunes. I was just listening to them; I couldn't play them. I was just going over the scales with it.
So this was in 1924.

Yeah. The only thing I could play in '24, I could play those marches. You see what I mean? I knew those marches that we'd been playing with that band that Professor Parson taught us to play. Now, he told me, he said, "I'm going to show you how to play Jazz, get you on to it."
Who said that?
Billy Young.
Oh, he wanted to teach you Jazz?
Yeah, because he could play it, too, you
Phillips - 6
know. He could play a nice trumpet.
Well, I'm getting ahead. But I remember one time you told me a story about how Willis Young, Billy Young used to get on Prez for playing too much Jazz.
Oh yeah. Uh-huh.
But that's something different.
Yeah.
So in other words, he was into Jazz himself, too.

Yeah, he was into it. He didn't mind to play. But Prez played ungodly Jazz! You know what I mean? I mean, it was all right for what we liked. But man, Prez... Just like now. Just like you take Miles and cats like that. They play way out sometimes. It's appreciated to a musician, but a lot of people don't...the public don't dig a lot of it sometimes, you know. But that's the way Prez was playing. He was just that far ahead of time. He was way ahead of time, man. He was a little boy with short pants on playin'. Said, "Look at that boy. He sure can play, can't he?" You know what I mean?
I'm getting ahead of myself, and I didn't mean to cut you off from where you were talking about. So you were back talking about Willis Young getting the people together, teaching you scales in 1924.
Yes.
Okay. So I'm going to let you get back on that.
Phillips - 7
Yeah. Well, he started teaching the scales and teaching the chords, and things like that. I'll never forget, he called it... What did he call it? Anyway, we'll let that go.
What's that?

Ain't nothin' but a chord change, but it was in a book... Semi-tone. He would teach us semi-tones. He called the chords in them days "semi-tones." He was teaching us those. Like, B-flat, E-flat, and A-flat.
Did he teach Prez this, too?

No. Prez could play it natural. Because he had a good talent to play that. When he'd play a solo, he played them in there anyway. I mean, that's where his ear could tell him to do that. We used to look at him, man, all the kids in the band... Because we was all kids together. Maybe I'm about three or four or five years older than Prez, something like that. But we was all together, and we used to look at him, man... We didn't call him Prez. We called him Bub. That's what his father... They called him Bub. Lee called him Bubba.
Lee is Lester's younger brother.
Yeah. He called him Bubba. And Irma, she called him Lester.
Irma, Lester's sister, called him Lester.
Yeah.
Phillips - 8
You were saying that their mother was still in Warren at that time.

Oh yeah. Sure. They had a big apartment that they rented there for the winter. Yeah, they stayed there until about March. They left, went on a show, one of them little shows. And he told us we was goin' on a big show.
Was this March of '24 or '25?
March of '24. [SO PREZ WAS 14] I didn't go with them, though, then. I didn't go with them until the 15th of April. That's when he sent for me.

Yeah. I went with him then. He went on a little show, a small... When we went, he was on a big show. We had a whole big Pullman car where his show stayed. The show traveled on a Pullman car. A show like that, you see there...
You showed me the photographs.
All them people stayed in a Pullman car.
He rented this Pullman car?
No. The show furnished it.
I see. Who ran the show? Who was in charge of the show?
The guy who had that show was named Billy Clark. Yeah, he owned the show.
So this was going on the TOBA circuit, right?
Oh, no! This was the carnival! We'd just
Phillips - 9

go from town to town and play this. Like, that picture was taken in Lexington, Kentucky, at the Kentucky State Fair. That's what we played. Fairs, played towns like... See, in that time, people didn't see nothin'. Wasn't no radio or TVs. So if they'd want to see a show, they'd come out and see it.
Right. I just want to identify that photograph. That's the photograph with Lester with his short pants on.
Yeah.
So as you were saying, he wanted you to go out, and they went out in March, and you didn't go out until April 15.
That's when he sent for me. He sent for four of us.
And those four people were?

Pete Jones, myself, my brother, and another cat played... We called him Ham, but his name was Jessie Hamilton. We went out with him. You know, that was a... Travelin' like that in a big Pullman car, with a cook, everything -- a kitchen and everything on there.
Excuse me. What did Jessie Hamilton play?
He played peck horn.
That's E-flat or something?
E-flat alto. He played peck horn, and he was a comedian, and he could dance. He was a good comedian. He was a better comedian than he was a musician.
What was your brother playing?
Phillips - 10
Bass. Then bass horn. Then he started...
You mean tuba?
Yeah.
Your brother was playing tuba.
Yeah.
And Jone was playing trombone, and you were playing trumpet at that time.
Yeah.
Were you already playing trumpet when Willis Young started to teach you scales? Or were you still playing the E-flat clarinet?
No, I was playing trumpet. Cornet then. I had quit playing the clarinet about a year or so before...
Before you knew...
Yeah, before him. What made me want to play the trumpet was when I heard Louis Armstrong playing "The St. Louis Blues" with Bessie Smith.
Okay. That was in 1924 or 1923?
That was in 1922 or 1923, somewhere right there.
When you first heard it...
Yeah, he was playing with Bessie Smith.
I think that was recorded in '23, if I'm not... Or maybe '24.
Oh, you remember the record.
Phillips - 11
Well, I remember the record, but I'm trying to think if the date is '23 or '24. But that's not important. The thing that's important is when you first heard it.
When I first heard it was 1924. No, 1922! That's right. [RECORDING DATE WAS JANUARY 14, 1925]
You're sure that's not a little early.
Wait a minute. '22... No.
Because I think she didn't start recording until '23.
Yeah, it was '23.
Anyway, that made you start playing cornet.
Yeah, that's when I wanted to play it then. I changed. I was playing E-flat clarinet in the band.
Then you started the cornet.

The cornet, yeah. From then, I used to get... My mother bought all them records. See, she bought a record of King Oliver playing with a team called Butterbeans and Susie. I don't know whether you ever heard of them.
A vaudeville team.

Vaudeville, yeah. He made some records with them, King Oliver did, with just nothing but him and the piano. That's the way Louis made this "St. Louis Blues." Ain't nobody but he and Fred Longshaw playing piano. Louis got a mute in it. That's the prettiest sound I think I ever heard in my life. It just drove me crazy to hear that. I used to just sit and listen to it all night. We had one of
Phillips - 12
them old things where you had to wind it up to play it, and it had a dog looking over the microphone.
A Victor.

A Victor, that's what it is. So I used to play it all the time. So then it got good. I kept blowing it, and I was getting pretty good on it. Then Mister Young told me... See, that's what we always called him. Mister Young told me that...
You were into the record before you knew Willis Young or after you knew Willis Young?
After.
So you knew Willis Young first.
Yeah.
So you probably were still playing the clarinet when you met Willis Young.

No. I was playing trumpet. Cornet. I was playing the cornet. But about along in the time when he came around my home, a little before that time... I guess about a year that I'd been playing it, playing the cornet.
So you heard that record before you knew Willis Young.

Yeah. And that's what made me want to play it good. Then he... You know how they tell you what you're going to do. He said, 'You go with me, I'm gonna get you a nice, pretty...' He had one of them Holden trumpets, a pretty one. 'I'm going to get you one of these, I'm going to get
Phillips - 13
you..."
A trumpet or a cornet?

A trumpet. The trumpet was just comin' out then. When I got with him there wasn't but a few people who had trumpets. He had one, because he had every kind of instrument that... All high-class instruments. C-Melody, gold plated -- they wasn't silver. He had silver and gold. He used silver playing for the carnivals and he used his gold playing for the vaudeville. He kept teaching and told me...

And he wrote me a letter and told me, "You be ready to leave the 15th of April." My mother said, "No, you can't go. You're too young to be going out in the world. I said, "Why? Why I'm too young?" She said, "You too young to go out in the world. I don't want you to go." I said, "Mama, as much as I'm goin' to have to go against what you're saying, I'm goin'." And he told my mother, too. He said, "You better let him go. Don't hold him back." Said "It's holdin' him back, stayin' around here. Let him get out that way, and hear people play and see people. That will give him more..." He was right. He told my mother. But she was a little square when it come to... She was just a home woman, raised children...
She didn't want you to go out.
She didn't want me to leave home. "You stay. You play all right here. You play in the church..."
Phillips - 14
She played all in them church. "Play in the church and that will be better," and all that stuff.
Your mother played organ in the church.
Yeah.
Did you have much exposure to church music yourself?

Yeah! You see, my mother taught us how to... See, I could read music when I first started playing. I know "do" was C and "re" was E, like that. Then I found out that when playing the horn, it's the same thing -- it's C-D-E-F-G-A-B-C. It was the same scale. So I liked that. Didn't have too hard a time learning, because I had a pretty good start, background. Then all I had to do was get out there and blow. Man, when I first started, man, you could hear me blowing for two miles -- on that carnival! Yeah, you had to blow loud outside.
We got on that show, and we went everywhere. We went traveling around. The show closed in Palatka, Florida.
How do you spell that?
I don't exactly know how to spell it right.
Palatka, Florida is where the first tour you were on with the Willis Young band ended. Is that right?
No, that's where the show closed. The carnival.
Okay, the carnival.
Phillips - 15
Then he got on vaudeville.
When was that when that first closed?
In 1924 about November.
So April to November you were with the show. The carnival.
Yeah.
And then in November you got into vaudeville.
Yeah. But he got back out of it, though.
And Prez was in there all that time, right?
Yeah!
Lee and Irma were in there, too?
That's right.
Lee must have been very young.
Yeah, Lee was about 10 or 11.

What kind of stuff was Lester listening to? Did he have any records at that time, in 1924, from April to November? You had the Louis Armstrong-Bessie Smith recording of "St. Louis Blues." Did you ever play that for him?
No.
What other things was he listening to? Because you mentioned all the things later on, Trumbauer and Beiderbecke, like "Singin' The Blues" and all of that. That wasn't even out at that time.
No.
So I was wondering what kind of stuff Lester was
Phillips - 16
listening to at that time.
Well, there wasn't too much to listen to then. Not until that music started coming out.
You mean until those later ones...
Yeah. Then they started... Well, we listened to the Dixieland Jazz Band.
You listened to the Original Dixieland Jazz Band?
The Original Dixieland Jazz Band.
Right. The one that recorded in 1917?
Yeah.
Did Lester used to listen to that?
Well, they still were making music in '24, you know.
Was Lester into that? Was he listening to that?

Yeah, we used to listen to them, different things. Then after that, we got together, Lester, Pete and myself... We used to get together and play Bix, Frankie Trumbauer... We played together, played it three-part harmony.
We'll get to that a little later, because that's a little later on. But at this time, in 1924, on that first carnival tour, Lester was not listening to records, or was he listening to records?
No, he wasn't listening to no records. Not then too much. You'd listen to what you'd hear.
Listen to what you hear. What kind of things...
Phillips - 17
We'd run into a lot of bands playing.
What kind of bands did you and Les and Jones hear at that time? What kind of people did you hear on the road? Also, what kind of music were they playing in the carnival show itself?
The carnival?
Yeah. And what kind of people did you run into, that you'd say were maybe influences or at least people to listen to?
Well, we'd run into people like Paul Whiteman, you know... They'd play in different places.
Would they allow Black people to go in and hear Paul Whiteman?
Well, we'd be playing something like a fair. See, them fairs we played, they'd be playing outside. You know what I mean? They'd be playing a concert. Paul Whiteman...
And everybody would get to hear it?
Sure. Because everybody could sit... In down South, you know, they got White people sit over here and the Black people sit here. Jim Crow, rather. But everybody would listen to the same music.
So you heard Paul Whiteman live in 1924?
No, I don't know. '24 or '25. Yeah, yeah, I heard him. Paul Whiteman, Vincent Lopez, and...who else at
Phillips - 18
that time? Ted Lewis. All them bands that I heard then, they was playin' that what you call ragtime jazz. Right after that, Fletcher Henderson was coming on.
In the mid-20's?
It must have been around about '23 or '24, somewhere around there.
He did record in '23. [1924]
Yeah.
He had Louis in there.
And Louis was with him, Don Redman... He had a hell of a band.
But as far as some of these shows that you heard, Ted Lewis, Vincent Lopez and Paul Whiteman, Lester Young used to go listen to them, too?
Yeah, we used to... Another band we used to go listen to at that time, Coon and Sam.
Coon Saunders? Yeah, I've heard of them.
You've heard of them?
Yeah.

Yeah. Coon and Saunders. We used to go to hear them. But see, we'd go to theatres... See, a lot of times we didn't have to be segregated because we was up in the northern states, like Nebraska, Kansas and Minnesota. See, these shows, these carnivals played all these towns too.
Was this in the first tour? The first carnival tour?
Phillips - 19
The one from April to November of '24?
Let me see the first one, the carnival tour...
That's all I'm trying to ask you about right now, because we'll get to the other stuff later.
Yeah. Well, the first carnival tour, we went to... Let's see, as far north as we went was Indianapolis.
Where did you mainly tour? You ended up in Florida, right?
Yeah.
What places did you cover on that tour, from April to November?
Well, we played... Like, sent down to Kentucky to them little small towns. Lexington, Kentucky. Bowling Green, Kentucky. Knoxville, Tennessee. Chattanooga, Tennessee. Roanoke, Virginia.
This was on that first tour?

Yeah, the first tour. Roanoke, Virginia. Flemington, Alabama, a little town... I never will forget when we played Harlan, Kentucky, because the policemen had to escort us from our car, escort us from where we lived, our Pullman car, to the show ground.
Were there troubles going on at that time?
Yeah, 'cause they didn't like Black people.
Phillips - 20
In Harlan?
Harlan, Kentucky. I'll never forget that.
That was on the first tour in 1924?

Yeah, mmm-hmm. Right. I'll never forget that day. They'd be callin' you all kind of names, "niggers" and all that stuff. So, you know, I'll never forget that. See, we had about six-seven girls on the show. They'd want to be feelin' at 'em, [GROWLS], all that stuff, you know.
The people who were reaching in to the train...
No! On the show.
Oh, on the show, grabbing at the girls.
Yeah. See, we made a bally... See, you don't know much about a carnival.
Tell me about that. In fact, tell me the whole show that they used to put on, if you can. As much as you can remember.

See, what you do, you come out on a bally, all the people, all the show come out on the front -- the band, too. They got a big platform out there you come out on. You come out there and you play -- the band plays. You play something like maybe "Running Wild" or something like that ... [SINGS]...that show beat. [SINGS] One of them show things, you know what I mean. See, people would be standin' around on the ground, looking, and this guy would be telling you... They got a spieler, he's tellin' about the show, "Come on in, it's a good show. There's a guy in there so funny til he made a
Phillips - 21
mule laugh," and all that shit. Then they people started comin' in. They'd come in and see the show. It was a good show. It wasn't a bad show! A good show. The band playing...
Then, when we'd get in there, before the show come on, we'd play a couple of tunes. The band.
What were some of those tunes? You mentioned "Running Wild."
Yeah, that's a tune... We played that out in front for the... Everybody would be dancing on that.
Well, a spieler, you say, would be out there calling...?
Yeah. "Hey! Hey! Come over here. This is where it is!"
That's the spieler.
Yeah. And he's... Some people call them spielers, some people call them barkers, like a dog barking -- call them a barker, yeah.
Then you got them inside, and what were the numbers that you played?

We'd get 'em inside... Well, we'd play them before the show opened up. See, the show had a curtain, they got a curtain and everything in there. But the people's back there, because the show's getting ready to hit, you know what I mean. Then we go up there and we play a couple of numbers while the people are comin' in. We'd play something like "The
Phillips - 22
"Wang-Wang Blues" and "How Come You Do Me Like You Do-Do-Do?", something like that. And Les, he would go crazy on that...
What was that?
"How Come You Do Me Like You Do-Do-Do?" "Yes, Sir, that's My Baby."
He was into improvising at that time?

Sure, man! You know what he'd play on "Yes Sir, That's My Baby"? He'd go ...[SINGS THEME STRAIGHT]... he played it ...[SINGS TYPICAL LESTER YOUNG IMPROVISATION]... And in those days you had slap tonguin'. You've heard that?
He was into slap tonguing?
Oh, he played all of everything. Everything a saxophone could be, he played it.
His style.. If he was improvising in 1924, what kind of style was he into? What kind of ideas did he have? I mean, you just gave us an example of something right there.
His own ideas. See, he was creative.
And he had not even heard Trumbauer or Beiderbecke or any of those people at that time...
Yeah, but he had a hell of a style!
He already was playing, improvising?
Yeah.
Do you know anybody that he would have listened to besides...? Were there any records he was into?
Well, there wasn't many cats out there
Phillips - 23
playin' nothin' in them days. You didn't have nothin' to listen to. They wasn't playin' nothin' he wanted to hear, because he was playin' more than they was playin'.
Where did he actually get the idea to improvise?

Well, he just started off that way. He played a march that way. Like, we used to play "Shouting Liza". You never played that. That's a march. [SINGS ARRANGEMENT UP TO LESTER YOUNG's SOLO AND THEN THE FIRST FEW BARS] That's when the old man said he was going to take him off the alto and put him on the tenor! Ha!
So he was already playing on the marches in 1924, then.
Sure! On the end of the trios, it's a pell mell at the end... Shit, man, he'd tear them up.
So he was already into that by the time you knew him. And that's the way he learned? Is that what you understood? The way he learned to improvise is by playing on marches?
Well, he learned... It was just within him to do that. Yeah, that's what it was; just him that played that way. Because anything he played, he improvised.
Anything he played he improvised.
Anything that he played, he gonna put something' to it and make it sound. He gonna dress it up, I'd say that. Yeah, he'd dress it up. Anything that he played, he would dress it up.
Well, later on, his father made him learn to read. Isn't
Phillips - 24
that right?
Yeah, he could read pretty good, but he wouldn't read like his father wanted him to read.
His father made him learn to read better.
Well, he made him read better. That picture you see. You see it? That picture of the band.
What year was that picture of Lester in the knee pants?
Oh, that was 1924.
What were you going to say about that picture, about him learning to read...?
He could read good when he got to the band.
He's already learned to read good by that time or after that time?
No, he could read pretty good, but he learned to read good in there because he was playing the first alto, and he had to...
He was a tenor in that photograph, right? He played a tenor?
On that show, yeah. But when he played the band, he played alto. He never did play tenor with his father's band.
So let me just get it straight. When you said the show, you're talking about the carnival.
Yeah, the carnival, that's what I'm talking
Phillips - 25
about.
And when you're saying the band, you're talking about the vaudeville?
No, I'm talking about the band. See, he had a band and a... See, this band picture I showed you wasn't in no show. We played dances. Went over the country playing dances.
This one with the mother...
No, not her. The other one.
Okay. But this picture was with his mother and his sister...
Oh yeah, that's the show.
That's the show. And they played carnivals?
Yeah, we worked on a carnival. It was a carnival.
I understand that. But you didn't get into vaudeville until November 1924.
Not that time. But he had been in vaudeville... They'd been in that before I ever met them.
Right. But you didn't get in...
I didn't get in...
Prez had already been doing vaudeville...
Been in vaudeville, sure. He and Lee and Irma had an act they did together.
On the TOBA circuit.
Phillips - 26
Yeah. Because they danced. Les could dance. They danced like hell. They could sing. Lee, all of them could dance.
Danced and sing.
Yeah.
When you talk about the band that you were in, they used to perform at...what was that?
Which one you mean?
I'm just trying to get it straight, so the people will know when you say show and when you say band.
Well, I mean the carnival. I'll say carnival, and that will make it better.
Carnival is the...?
Carnival is the one there.
So that's the show?
Carnival. I said show, I called it, but...
When you say "carnival," you mean "show."

wanted me to go with him.

Yeah, head arrangements. Like 'Tiger Rag,' the Blues, some kind of movement on the Blues -- there was all kind of Blues. Then we'd have like 'How Come You Do Me Like You Do' -- those kind of easy sleevin' tunes.
You'd know them by the head.
Yeah.
Any interesting comments that Louis Jordan made that you might want to pass on?

Oh, he was a nice guy. He was a really nice guy. He was just about as nice a fellow as you'd want to meet. Because, see, I didn't know him too much in Arkansas, because he lived in one part of Arkansas and I lived in

another; he lived in northern Arkansas and I lived in southern Arkansas. But anyway, he used to come to my home all the time on his Daddy's show...
To Warren, Arkansas.
Yeah.
The Rabbit Foot Minstrel Show.
That's right.
I guess it was a really influential little group at that time.

Oh yeah. We were playing everything. He was playing then "Caledonia," "Choo-Choo Cha-Boogie," "Slender, Tender and Tall," "Salt Pork, West Virginia," "Ain't Nobody Here But Us Chickens," "I'm Gonna Move to The Outskirts of Town" -- that's the tune that made him. If you went to a dance, you didn't have to play too much, because you'd play "I'm Gonna Move..." -- man, he'd play that for about an hour. And them people still... Especially when you'd go down South, they'd be screamin' and hollerin' about that, because that's the Blues! People down South understand the Blues. They know the Blues. Like me, I know the Blues. Was Lester Young a big fan of the Blues? I know King Oliver certainly was.
Yeah.

Did Lester Young ever have any interesting things to say about Blues playing?
Yeah, he loved it.
[PAUSE; TELEPHONE]
Les loved the Blues. It was like he said...
Do you have any quotes? That's what I mean.

No. We just always said that if you can play the Blues good, you can play Jazz. See, because Blues is the fundamental of Jazz. See, when you've got that Blues feelin' and that same feelin', just like you take a Seventh chord and a minor chord, those are blue notes. Make those, and then see... See, there's just a lot of people don't have the feeling to play the Blues. It's like I got a brother; he can't play no Blues.
Which brother?

Clarence also played with Ma Rainey.
Yeah. But I never seen him then. All that was away from me, because I stayed away from... See, I didn't see Clarence for about ten years one time. He was away from me.
Let me ask you this about the Blues. I've always been taught that Blues have different styles from different areas, and what you have in Mississippi and Arkansas is one thing,
Phillips - 215
and what you have in Texas is a little bit different. Like, T-Bone Walker, what he came out with in Texas was a little bit different than, say, what Muddy Waters would have brought from Mississippi.
They might have had some different words.
I mean, different kinds of harmonies. And some of them were into Jazz rhythms and stuff.
Well, it's like that, too.
I just wondered if you noticed any differences when you were growing up, what you heard in Arkansas and what you heard in other places.
The real Blues that I heard is Bessie Smith, Ma Rainey, all them -- those are the Blues that I know. This sophisticated Blues... I'm talking the real Blues.
Sophisticated stuff like all the way up to Nat Cole... He put a lot of changes in there.
Yeah.
Of course, you played with Ivory Joe Hunter.
Yeah.
He was into Blues a lot.
Oh yeah. And he did sweet tunes, too. "I Lost My Baby and Almost Lost My Mind" -- that's the one that made him.

Giggin'.

And you were in that group.
